prompt: Write a literature review of about 300 words on how evening social media use relates to adolescent sleep quality.
text:
Research on adolescent sleep has increasingly focused on digital media, particularly the use of smartphones and social networking sites during the hours before bedtime. Early studies relied on self-reported measures and cross-sectional surveys, which established a consistent association between late-night screen use and shorter sleep duration. However, these designs could not determine whether media use caused sleep problems or whether adolescents with existing sleep difficulties were simply more likely to turn to their phones at night.

Longitudinal work has begun to address this limitation. Several panel studies tracking teenagers over one to two years found that increases in evening messaging predicted later delays in sleep onset, even after controlling for baseline mood and academic stress. Researchers have proposed a few mechanisms to explain this pattern. The most frequently cited is the displacement hypothesis, which holds that time spent online replaces sleep, while the arousal hypothesis suggests that emotionally engaging content keeps the nervous system active when it should be winding down. Blue light exposure has also been examined, although the evidence for its direct effect on melatonin in real-world settings is weaker than laboratory findings suggest.

A smaller body of research complicates the picture by distinguishing between types of use. Studies that separate passive scrolling from interactive communication report that the latter is less consistently linked to poor sleep, possibly because it reflects social connection rather than compulsive checking. Differences in gender and age also emerge, with older adolescents and girls often showing stronger associations. Taken together, the literature points to a relationship that is real but conditional, and it suggests that interventions targeting the content and timing of use may be more effective than blanket restrictions.

prompt: Write 3 paragraphs for a lit review on remote work and employee wellbeing.
text:
Remote work became much more common after 2020 and a lot of research has been done on how it affects employees wellbeing. Early studies often found that people who worked from home reported higher job satisfaction and less stress, mostly because they had more control over their schedule and didnt have to commute. But these studies were usually done during the pandemic, when people had no choice and also had to deal with home schooling and other problems, so its hard to say if the results apply to normal remote work.

More recent papers look at a different side of the issue. Some researchers found that remote workers feel more isolated and report loneliness more often than office workers, especially if they live alone. Others looked at boundaries between work and home life. When there is no clear line between the office and the living room, people tend to work longer hours and check emails late at night, which can lead to burnout. A few studies also say that managers who cant see their staff may trust them less, and this can make employees feel pressure to prove they are working.

The evidence is mixed overall. Most authors agree that the effect depends on the person and the job, and on how the company supports them. Hybrid arrangements seem to get the best results in many surveys, but there arent many long term studies to confirm this. For my own project I think the most useful thing would be to look at how organisations set rules about working hours, because that seems to matter more than the location itself.

prompt: Write a literature review section on microfinance and women's empowerment.
text:
Microfinance has been widely promoted as a tool for empowering women in developing countries since the 1990s. Many scholars have studied whether access to small loans really change women's position in their households and communities. The early research was very optimistic, and many reports showed that women who receive loans have more control over spending and are more respected by their husbands. However, later studies have questioned these findings, because the loans are often controlled by male relatives, and women only act as a channel for the money rather than as the real owner of the business.

Another important theme in the literature is the difference between economic empowerment and social empowerment. Some authors argue that increase of income does not automatically lead to more freedom of movement or decision making in family matters. For example, a study in Bangladesh found that women who joined group lending programs had higher income, but they still needed permission from their husband to leave the house. Other researchers have focused on the role of the group meetings, which give women a space to talk about problems and build confidence together. These social effects seems to be stronger than the financial effects in some cases.

Recent work also pay more attention to the risks of over indebtedness. When women take loans to pay off earlier debts, the outcome can be negative, and the situation may bring more stress to the family. Because of this, many researchers now suggest that microfinance should be combined with training, savings products and legal education. In my opinion, this literature shows that the impact of microfinance depends very much on the local context and on the design of the program.

prompt: Write a literature review on urban green space and community cohesion for a sociology module.
text:
The relationship between urban green space and community cohesion has attracted sustained scholarly attention across sociology, environmental psychology and urban planning. Foundational studies in the late twentieth century, notably those examining public housing in Chicago, suggested that vegetated common areas facilitated informal interaction among neighbours, thereby strengthening social ties and collective efficacy. Subsequent quantitative research has broadly supported this proposition, although the magnitude of the effect varies considerably with the quality, accessibility and design of the spaces concerned.

A central methodological debate concerns the direction of causality. Cross-sectional analyses frequently find that residents of greener neighbourhoods report higher levels of trust, yet these areas may also be wealthier or more stable, confounding the apparent relationship. Recent quasi-experimental studies, including several exploiting the staggered greening of vacant lots in American cities, have attempted to isolate the intervention effect. Their findings indicate modest but statistically significant increases in outdoor use and reported neighbourly contact, particularly among older residents and households with children.

The literature also highlights the mediating role of usage patterns. Parks that host structured programmes, such as community gardening or organised sports, appear to generate stronger cohesion than passive open space. Conversely, green areas perceived as unsafe may reduce social contact, suggesting that vegetation alone is insufficient. Future research would benefit from longitudinal designs capable of tracking cohesion over time and from closer attention to variations between cultural contexts, since findings from North American cities may not transfer directly to dense European or rapidly urbanising Asian settings.

prompt: Write a short lit review on the gig economy and job security.
text:
Okay so the gig economy has gotten a huge amount of attention in the research over the last decade, and honestly the picture is pretty messy. A lot of early papers were super excited about it. The idea was that people could pick their own hours, make some extra cash, and be their own boss. Studies from the US and UK found that many gig workers liked the flexibility, and some said it was better than a bad retail job they had before. That's the optimistic side anyway.

But then you get the researchers who look at job security, and they're way less happy. Gig workers usually don't get sick pay, pensions, or any protection if the app suddenly cuts their hours or changes the pay rate. A few papers show that income can swing a lot from week to week, which makes budgeting really hard. Some also point out that platforms control the rules through algorithms, so workers can get deactivated without much explanation. That kind of uncertainty is a big deal, and it can cause stress even for people who are doing fine on paper.

What I find interesting is that the debate isn't just about whether gig work is good or bad. It's more about who is doing it. Students and people with a second income seem to be happy with it, while people who depend on it for their main living are the ones who struggle. Some researchers now argue that the real question is how much protection platform workers should get, and there's a growing push for things like minimum pay rules in places like the EU. Still, there aren't many long term studies yet, so we don't really know how this will shake out.

prompt: Write the introduction and discussion for a lab report on the effect of temperature on catalase activity.
text:
Enzymes are biological catalysts that accelerate chemical reactions by lowering the activation energy required for substrate conversion. Catalase, which is found in nearly all aerobic organisms, decomposes hydrogen peroxide into water and oxygen, and its activity can be measured by monitoring the rate of gas evolution. Because enzymes are proteins, their catalytic performance is strongly influenced by temperature. At low temperatures, molecular motion is limited and reaction rates are slow, whereas moderate warming typically increases the frequency of productive collisions between enzyme and substrate. Beyond an optimum, however, thermal energy disrupts the hydrogen bonds and hydrophobic interactions that maintain the three-dimensional structure of the enzyme, leading to denaturation and a sharp loss of activity. The aim of this experiment was to determine the temperature at which bovine liver catalase showed maximum activity and to characterise the shape of the activity curve between 0 and 70 degrees Celsius.

The results broadly followed the expected pattern. Reaction rates increased from 0 to approximately 37 degrees Celsius, reaching a maximum near 40 degrees, before declining steeply at higher temperatures. The sharp fall in activity above 50 degrees is consistent with thermal denaturation, and the fact that rates at 60 and 70 degrees were close to zero suggests that most of the enzyme had lost its tertiary structure. The optimum temperature obtained here is slightly higher than the 37 degrees often reported for mammalian enzymes in vivo, which may reflect the short incubation time used in the assay. Enzyme stability over longer periods is usually lower at elevated temperatures, so a longer exposure would likely have shifted the apparent optimum downwards.

Several sources of error should be acknowledged. Gas volumes were read from a graduated syringe, and small leaks or bubbles may have introduced random error of around 2 to 3 millilitres. The temperature of the reaction mixture was measured once at the start of each trial and may have drifted during the measurement period. Future work could address these limitations by using a pressure transducer to record gas evolution continuously and by pre-equilibrating substrate and enzyme at each temperature before mixing.

prompt: Write intro and discussion for a lab report on how pH affects yeast fermentation.
text:
Yeast is a single celled fungus that carries out fermentation, turning sugar into carbon dioxide and ethanol. Fermentation is used in bread making and brewing, and it is also a good way to see how enzymes work in living cells. The enzymes in yeast work best in a certain pH range, because pH changes the charge on the amino acids in the enzyme and can change its shape. If the solution is too acidic or too alkaline the enzymes might stop working properly. In this experiment we wanted to find out how different pH levels affect the rate of CO2 production. We predicted that the rate would be highest around pH 5 to 6, which is close to what is normal for yeast.

The results showed that the gas production was highest at pH 5 and lowest at pH 9. At pH 3 there was some fermentation but it was slower than at pH 5. This fits with our prediction because yeast enzymes are adapted to slightly acidic conditions. The drop at pH 9 is probably because the enzymes were denatured or the yeast cells had trouble taking in glucose. Our graph shows a clear peak which makes the result easy to read, but there was alot of variation between the three repeats at pH 7, so we should be careful about saying exactly where the peak is.

There were some problems with the experiment. We used a measuring cylinder to collect the gas and the bubbles sometimes stuck to the sides, so the readings might be a bit low. We also did not check the temperature of the water bath during the whole time, and the temperature could have changed a little. If we did it again we would use a gas syringe or a balance to measure mass loss, and we would repeat each pH at least five times. It would also be useful to test more pH values between 4 and 6 to find the optimum more accurately.

prompt: Write intro and discussion for a plant biology lab report on UV-B exposure and bean seedling growth.
text:
Plants need light for photosynthesis, but the ultraviolet part of sunlight is usually considered harmful to plant tissue. UV-B radiation, in particular, can damage DNA and proteins, and it may reduce plant height and leaf area. However, many plants also produce protective compounds such as flavonoids when they are exposed to UV, and this response can make them more resistant to later stress. The purpose of this experiment is to examining how different daily doses of UV-B affect the growth of bean seedlings over fourteen days. We hypothesize that moderate UV exposure will reduce biomass gain, but that high exposure will cause more severe damage.

The data show that seedlings in the control group grew faster than seedlings in both UV treatments. The high dose group had the smallest leaves and the lowest dry weight at the end of the experiment. There was a difference between the low dose and control groups, but it was not statistically significant. This suggests that the damage is dose dependent, and that the lower dose may be below the threshold where growth is strongly affected. Some leaves in the high dose group showed brown spots, which is a common sign of tissue damage. It is possible that the plants uses more energy for repair and therefore had less energy left for growth.

In our opinion, the results support the hypothesis, although there are several limitations. We used only one species and only one growing period, so the results cannot be generalized to all plants. The lamps also produced some heat, and the temperature in the high dose chamber was about two degrees higher than in the control chamber, which may have contributed to the difference. In the future, the experiment should be repeated with better temperature control and with more replicates. It would also be interesting to measure flavonoid content directly.

prompt: Write the introduction and discussion for a chemistry lab report on recrystallisation of benzoic acid in different solvents.
text:
Recrystallisation is a purification technique based on the difference in solubility of a compound at elevated and ambient temperatures. An ideal solvent dissolves the target compound readily when hot but poorly when cold, while impurities remain either insoluble or fully soluble throughout the cooling process. The principle that like dissolves like provides a useful starting point for solvent selection, since polar solutes tend to dissolve in polar solvents and non-polar solutes in non-polar ones. Benzoic acid, which contains both a polar carboxyl group and a non-polar aromatic ring, presents an interesting case because its solubility in water is modest but increases considerably with temperature. This experiment compared the recovery yield of benzoic acid recrystallised from water, ethanol and a 1:1 ethanol-water mixture, with the aim of identifying the solvent that offered the best balance between purity and recovery.

The highest recovery was obtained from pure water, at 71 percent, while ethanol gave a considerably lower yield of 48 percent. This outcome may appear counterintuitive given that ethanol is generally a better solvent for aromatic acids at room temperature. However, the high solubility of benzoic acid in ethanol even when cold means that a greater proportion of the product remains in the mother liquor. The mixed solvent system gave an intermediate yield of 63 percent, which is consistent with a solvent whose cold solubility lies between those of its components. The melting points of the recovered crystals were all within two degrees of the literature value, indicating that purity was not substantially compromised by the choice of solvent in this range.

Several sources of loss should be noted. Some material was inevitably retained on the filter paper and the glassware during transfer, and the cooling rate was not controlled, which may have produced smaller crystals that passed through the filter more readily. Future investigations might quantify solubility at multiple temperatures to construct a solubility curve, which would allow a more rigorous prediction of optimal solvent composition.

prompt: Write intro and discussion for a biology lab on light intensity and photosynthesis rate in pondweed.
text:
Photosynthesis is the process plants use to turn light, water and carbon dioxide into sugar and oxygen, and it is one of the most important reactions on the planet. Light intensity is usually a limiting factor, which means that when light goes up, the rate goes up too, but only until something else like CO2 or temperature becomes the bottleneck. A common way to measure this in class is to put pondweed in water and count the oxygen bubbles it gives off in a set time. This experiment looked at how the rate changed when the lamp was moved closer to the plant, with the goal of finding the point where the curve starts to flatten out.

Our main result was pretty clear. Bubble count went up as the lamp got closer, from around 4 bubbles a minute at 100 cm to about 38 at 10 cm. The curve got flatter near the closest distances, which makes sense because the plant was probably running out of CO2 by then. The spread between repeats was kind of big at the middle distances, so we can't say the exact shape of the curve with much confidence. Also counting bubbles is pretty rough since some of them were tiny and we might have missed them.

If we did it again I'd want a gas syringe or a proper gas collection set up, because counting is so subjective. Lamp heat was also a problem. The water near the lamp got warmer, and warmer water holds less dissolved gas, so that might have changed the results. We could have used a heat filter or put a thermometer in the beaker. Still, the overall trend fits what the textbook says, so the experiment did what it was meant to do, even if the data isn't perfect.

prompt: Write a reflective journal entry on a six-week internship in a hospital administration office.
text:
My placement in the outpatient administration office at St Helen's Hospital began on a Monday morning with a short induction that covered patient records, scheduling systems and confidentiality rules. I had expected the work to be mostly clerical, and to some extent it was, but I was surprised by how much of the daily routine depended on coordination between departments. A single missing referral form could delay a clinic appointment by weeks, so much of my time was spent following up with GPs and specialist teams. Reflecting on the first two weeks, I think my early assumption that administration was separate from patient care was mistaken. The people at the front desk were often the first point of contact for anxious patients, and their tone and patience clearly shaped how families experienced the hospital.

A significant learning moment came when I was asked to help reconcile a backlog of cancelled appointments. I initially worked through the list in order of date, but my supervisor pointed out that urgent oncology referrals should be prioritised regardless of their position in the queue. This taught me that administrative systems carry clinical consequences, and that accuracy and judgement matter as much as speed. I also became more aware of how much I rely on written procedures without questioning them, and I plan to pay more attention to the reasons behind a process in future placements.

Looking back, the most valuable part of the internship was the opportunity to observe how different staff members managed pressure. Some relied on informal networks to get things done, while others followed the formal protocols strictly. Neither approach was consistently better. For my own development, I need to become more confident in asking questions when I am unsure, rather than waiting for someone to notice a mistake. The experience has convinced me that I want to pursue a career in health services management, and I have started reading about quality improvement methods to build on what I learned.

prompt: Reflective journal on your marketing internship at a small company.
text:
During my eight weeks at Brightline Digital I was basically the marketing intern, which mostly meant I did whatever nobody else had time for. My first week was a bit overwhelming. I got access to the company's social media accounts, a shared drive with about 400 files, and a list of things the manager wanted done by Friday. I didn't really know what the priorities were, so I asked a lot of questions, which I think was the right move even if it felt annoying at the time. Looking back, I should have asked earlier about what success looked like for each task, because I spent two days on a blog post that nobody ended up using.

The part I learned the most from was running the email newsletter. I had only done this in a class project before, so I wasnt sure how to measure whether it was working. My supervisor showed me how to look at open rates and click through rates, and she explained that a high open rate doesnt mean much if nobody clicks. We changed the subject lines and split the list into two groups, and the click rate went up a bit in the second month. It was a small thing but I felt proud of it, and it made me realise that marketing is more about testing ideas than having good ideas.

Some things didnt go well. I made a mistake in a post that had the wrong launch date, and it went out to about 2,000 people before I noticed. My manager was pretty calm about it but I felt really embarrassed. Next time I will check everything twice and ask for a second pair of eyes before anything gets published. Overall I think the internship was useful, mainly because I now know what kind of work I actually enjoy, which is writing and analysing results, not so much managing the social calendar.

prompt: Write a reflective journal on an engineering internship with a water utility.
text:
In this reflective journal I want to think about my internship at the municipal water utility in Tbilisi, where I worked for three months in the planning department. Before I started, I thought engineering was mostly about calculations and design software. However, during my first weeks I learned that most of the work are about meeting people and understanding what happens in the real network. My supervisor took me to several pumping stations, and I saw how old pipes were leaking in some districts. This experience was very different from the university lab, where everything was clean and predictable. I felt both excited and a little worried that I did not know enough to make a good contribution.

One project that I worked on was the analysis of water pressure in a residential area. I was asked to use the hydraulic model to find where pressure dropped below the minimum level during the evening peak. At first I made a mistake because I used the average daily demand instead of the peak hour demand. My supervisor explained the error patiently and said that engineers must always check their assumption before presenting results. I was embarrassed, but it was a useful lesson. Now I always ask myself which scenario the decision really depends on.

Working in a public institution also taught me about communication. Many residents were angry about interruptions in the supply, and the staff had to explain technical issues in simple words. I learned that a good engineer must listen carefully and not only present numbers. I hope that in my future career I will be able to combine technical skill with this kind of patience. The internship gave me more confidence, and I now think that I would like to work on infrastructure projects after graduation, especially those that improve services for poorer neighbourhoods.

prompt: Write a reflective journal entry on a legal internship at a law firm.
text:
This reflective entry considers my ten-week placement as a trainee clerk at Harrow and Lindqvist, a mid-sized commercial law firm. My principal responsibilities involved conducting document reviews for due diligence exercises, preparing bundles for hearings and drafting routine correspondence under supervision. In the initial stages, I found the volume of material overwhelming, and my early reviews were slower and less consistent than those of more experienced colleagues. Reflecting on this period, I recognise that my difficulty stemmed partly from an insufficient understanding of how individual documents related to the transaction as a whole. Once I began to read the matter summaries before commencing reviews, my accuracy improved considerably.

A particularly instructive episode occurred when I identified an ambiguous indemnity clause during a review of supplier agreements. I raised the issue with the supervising associate, who explained the commercial background that had led to the drafting choice. The exchange demonstrated that legal analysis is inseparable from its context, and that apparently technical wording often reflects negotiated compromises. It also highlighted the importance of raising concerns promptly and clearly, even when one is unsure whether they will prove significant.

On reflection, the placement has clarified my professional priorities. I found the precision and analytical discipline of the work rewarding, although I am less certain that I wish to pursue a career in transactional practice. I intend to seek opportunities in litigation support during the next academic year in order to test that preference. I am grateful to the firm for the candour and patience with which my colleagues responded to my questions, and I believe the experience has strengthened both my technical competence and my professional judgement.

prompt: Reflective journal on your summer internship at a museum.
text:
Okay so this is my reflection on the summer I spent as an education intern at the city history museum. I went in thinking I'd mostly be stuck behind a desk photocopying things, and honestly I was wrong about that. Most of my time was spent running school tours and making activity sheets for kids. The first tour was a disaster. I talked way too fast, I forgot half of what I'd practised, and one kid asked me a question about medieval armour that I totally couldn't answer. But by the end of the summer I was doing the tours solo and I actually enjoyed them, which still surprises me.

What I learned most is that you can't just read off a script and expect kids to care. The best moments happened when I stopped talking and let them touch the replica pottery or argue about what an object was used for. My supervisor, Dana, kept telling me to ask open questions instead of quiz questions, and at first I didn't get the difference. Once I did, the whole thing changed. I'd say things like what do you think this was for, and then just wait, even when the silence felt awkward. Weirdly, that silence was where the good stuff happened.

I also got a bit of a reality check about the job side of things. Museum education is badly paid and most of the positions are on short contracts, and a few of the staff were pretty open about how stressful that is. It made me think harder about whether this is something I want to do long term or just something I enjoy as a side thing. Right now I'm leaning towards doing it part time while I do a teaching certificate. Either way, I'm glad I went. Dana said she'd write me a reference, so that's something.

prompt: Write a book report on Pride and Prejudice.
text:
Jane Austen's Pride and Prejudice, first published in 1813, follows the Bennet family of Longbourn, whose five unmarried daughters face the prospect of financial insecurity because their estate is entailed to a distant cousin. The novel is structured around the courtship between Elizabeth Bennet and Fitzwilliam Darcy, whose initial mutual hostility stems from misjudgements on both sides. Elizabeth's quick wit and readiness to form opinions contrast with Darcy's reserve and sense of social rank, and much of the narrative's pleasure lies in watching each character revise their assumptions in light of new evidence. Austen uses free indirect discourse to let the reader inhabit Elizabeth's perspective, which makes her eventual recognition of her own prejudice feel earned rather than convenient.

The novel is also a sharp study of class and marriage as economic institutions. Mrs Bennet's anxious scheming, Mr Collins's obsequious proposal and Charlotte Lucas's pragmatic acceptance of him all reveal how little choice women had in securing their futures. Austen does not present these characters simply as comic figures, however. Charlotte's decision is treated with a degree of understanding, and the novel makes clear that marriage without affection can be a survival strategy rather than a moral failure. The tension between romantic ideals and material necessity runs throughout the book and gives it a depth that is easy to overlook beneath its comedy.

I would recommend this novel to readers who enjoy character driven fiction and careful social observation. Its humour is dry and precise, and its ending, while conventional in its outcome, feels satisfying because the characters have genuinely changed. My main criticism is that some secondary plot threads, particularly those involving Lydia and Wickham, are resolved rather quickly and conveniently. Even so, the central relationship remains one of the most carefully constructed in English fiction.

prompt: Book report on 1984 by George Orwell.
text:
1984 by George Orwell is about a man named Winston Smith who lives in Airstrip One, which is part of a country called Oceania. The Party runs everything and there is a leader called Big Brother who is on posters everywhere. Winston works at the Ministry of Truth where he changes old newspaper articles so they match what the Party says is true at the moment. He hates the Party but he is scared to show it, so he starts a secret diary, which is a crime. The book is written in third person but we only really see things from Winston's point of view, so we dont always know what other characters are thinking.

The main plot is about Winston's relationship with Julia. They meet secretly and start an affair, which is also illegal because the Party wants people to have no private feelings. They rent a room above a shop and think they are safe, but in the end they are caught by the Thought Police. The part with O'Brien is the most important for me. Winston thinks O'Brien is part of a resistance group, but he is really working for the Party. Then O'Brien tortures Winston in the Ministry of Love until he believes that two plus two can equal five. I found this part really disturbing, and I think it is the point of the whole book, which is that the Party can control what people think as well as what they do.

I think 1984 is still important today because of how it talks about surveillance, propaganda and fake news. The telescreens are like phones and social media that collect data about us. Orwell wrote it in 1948 but it still feels relevant, which is why it is on so many school reading lists. Some parts are a bit slow, especially the long section from Goldstein's book, which is basically a political essay inside a novel. Overall it is a very bleak book but I think everyone should read it at least once, because it makes you think about how easily freedom can be lost.

prompt: Write a book report on Things Fall Apart.
text:
Things Fall Apart is a novel written by the Nigerian author Chinua Achebe and published in 1958. The story is about Okonkwo, a respected man in the Igbo village of Umuofia. Okonkwo is very strong and hard working, and he wants to become the opposite of his father. His father, Unoka, was a poor man who was lazy and who did not take titles, so Okonkwo spends his whole life trying to be different from him. He fears to show weakness, and this fear make him act violently even against his own family, especially his son Nwoye. In my opinion, Okonkwo is a tragic character because his strength is also the thing that destroys him.

The novel is interesting because it shows the Igbo culture in detail before the arrival of European missionaries and colonial administration. Achebe describe religious ceremonies, marriage customs, farming seasons and the justice system of the village. These details are important because they show that the society has its own rules and values, and it is not primitive as some colonial writers said in the past. When the missionaries come, some people, including Nwoye, begin to convert to Christianity. This divide the community and cause a crisis that Okonkwo cannot control. The ending is very sad, because Okonkwo kills himself rather than accept the humiliation of being arrested by the colonial officers.

I recommend this book to students who want to understand African literature and the effects of colonialism. The language is simple but the ideas are complex. Achebe uses many Igbo proverbs, which help the reader feel the wisdom of the culture. At first I found the proverbs confusing, but after some pages I start to understand their meaning. The book taught me that a story can change how people see a whole continent, and that is why I think it is still one of the most important novels of the twentieth century.

prompt: Write a critical book report on Middlemarch.
text:
George Eliot's Middlemarch, published in serial form between 1871 and 1872, offers a panoramic study of provincial English society in the years preceding the Reform Act of 1832. Its central figures, Dorothea Brooke and Tertius Lydgate, are idealists whose ambitions are gradually compromised by the constraints of marriage, reputation and money. Dorothea's aspiration to contribute to some great and noble work, expressed in the novel's celebrated opening, establishes a tension between the private longing for significance and the public world that frustrates it. Lydgate's scientific aims meet a similar fate, as his reforming zeal is eroded by financial obligation and the suspicions of his community. The narrative therefore engages seriously with the question of how individual moral energy survives within social institutions.

Eliot's narrator is a distinctive presence, frequently intervening to generalise about human nature and to reflect on the limits of perception. These interventions can appear discursive to modern readers, yet they are integral to the novel's ethical project, which insists that ordinary lives deserve the same attention as heroic ones. The multiplicity of plots, including the Bulstrode banking scandal and the uncertain status of Will Ladislaw, produces a structure in which causality is distributed across many characters rather than concentrated in a single protagonist. This distribution enacts the novel's argument that a community is an interdependent web of consequences.

Middlemarch is demanding, and its length and density reward patient reading. Its treatment of marriage in particular remains morally searching, since Eliot refuses either to condemn Dorothea's disappointment or to present it as the whole of her story. The closing lines, which suggest that the unhistoric acts of ordinary people form the basis of a better world, may strike some readers as sentimental. Nevertheless, the novel's sustained attention to the gap between intention and outcome provides a rigorous and humane account of moral life that continues to repay critical reflection.

prompt: Write a short book report on The Great Gatsby.
text:
So The Great Gatsby is one of those books everybody says you have to read, and I was kind of dreading it, but honestly it's way shorter than I expected and way more fun. It's set in the summer of 1922 on Long Island, and the narrator is Nick Carraway, a young guy who moves next door to a huge mansion where a mysterious man named Jay Gatsby throws massive parties every weekend. Nick gets pulled into Gatsby's world, and slowly we find out that Gatsby is obsessed with Daisy, Nick's cousin, who he knew years ago before she married the rich and cheating Tom Buchanan. The whole book kind of runs on that obsession.

What I liked most is how the parties are described. They're glamorous but also kind of empty, with people who don't even know the host and just come to drink and gossip. Fitzgerald makes the whole scene feel dazzling and sad at the same time. And the green light at the end of Daisy's dock is such a simple image but it sticks with you. Gatsby keeps reaching for it, like the past is something he can get back if he wants it badly enough. That's the big theme for me, the idea that the American dream is about chasing something you can never quite grab.

The ending hit hard. I won't spoil the details, but let's just say it's not a happy one and some of the characters are pretty awful about it. Nick is kind of a weird narrator too, because he judges people but also keeps hanging around them. I wasn't sure I liked him at first. Still, I'd say this is worth the read even if you're not usually into old books. It's short, the writing is really good, and it'll make you think about what you'd do to get the life you want.

prompt: Write a business case analysis of Blockbuster and Netflix.
text:
Blockbuster was once the dominant video rental chain in the United States, operating thousands of stores at its peak in the early 2000s. Its decline and the rise of Netflix are frequently cited as a textbook case of disruption, yet a closer analysis suggests that the outcome was shaped by specific strategic choices rather than inevitability alone. This case examines the company's decision making between 2000 and 2010, focusing on its response to the emergence of mail order DVD rental and later streaming technology. The central question is why an industry leader with substantial resources failed to adapt to a business model that offered customers greater convenience at lower cost.

Blockbuster's principal weakness lay in its reliance on late fees as a revenue source, which generated substantial income but created customer resentment and a misaligned incentive structure. When Netflix introduced a flat subscription model without late charges, it offered a value proposition that directly addressed this grievance. Blockbuster did experiment with its own online service and a kiosk business, but these initiatives were treated as supplements to the store network rather than as a replacement for it. The company's large fixed cost base, including leases on physical locations, made it difficult to reallocate capital toward digital distribution without damaging short term profitability. Management also underestimated the speed at which broadband adoption would reduce the advantages of physical retail.

Several recommendations follow from this analysis. Incumbents facing disruptive entrants should separate new business units from legacy operations so that the new model is not constrained by the economics of the old one. They should also evaluate their revenue sources critically, asking whether profits derived from customer frustration are sustainable over time. Finally, decision makers should establish leading indicators, such as streaming subscriber growth and online usage trends, that signal when a strategic pivot is necessary rather than waiting for declining sales to make the case for change.

prompt: Business case analysis: should a family bakery open a second shop?
text:
Sweet Rise Bakery is a small family run business in a town of about 40,000 people. It has one shop that sells bread, pastries and cakes, and it makes most of its money on weekend mornings. The owner, Mrs Hasan, wants to open a second shop in the business district, which is about 15 minutes away by car. The question for this case is whether the expansion is a good idea, and if so how it should be financed and managed. The bakery has about 800 regular customers according to the loyalty card data, and its profit margin has been around 12 percent for the last two years.

Looking at the numbers, the expansion looks possible but risky. The new shop would cost around 180,000 in fit out and equipment, and the lease would be 2,500 a month. Mrs Hasan has 60,000 in savings, so she would need a bank loan for the rest. The main problem is that the first shop depends a lot on her being there every morning, and she does not have a reliable manager yet. If she spreads herself too thin, quality could fall and the original shop might lose customers. Also the business district has more office workers who buy coffee but not many cakes, so the product mix would probably need to change.

My recommendation is that Sweet Rise should delay the expansion for about a year. In that time it could hire and train a store manager, test a smaller counter in the business district using a pop up or a partnership with a cafe, and build a better understanding of what those customers want. If the test works, the bakery would have much better evidence for the bank and a stronger case for the loan. I think this is safer than borrowing a large amount now and hoping the new location will recieve enough customers to pay for itself.

prompt: Write a business case analysis of an airline's pricing strategy.
text:
This case analyse the pricing strategy of a regional airline that operate short haul flights between three cities in Eastern Europe. The airline has recently faced stronger competition from low cost carriers, and its load factor has fall from 82 percent to 71 percent over the past year. Management is considering whether to reduce fares on its most popular routes or to introduce a more complex system of fare classes. The company has around 14 aircraft and its operating costs are relatively high because of an older fleet and union agreements with pilots and cabin crew. In this analysis, we will examine the financial situation, the market structure and the options available to the management.

The main problem is that the airline has tried to compete on price without a clear cost advantage. When it lowered fares by 15 percent on one route, the passenger number increased, but the revenue per seat did not improve enough to cover the extra costs. Some business travellers, who are usually less sensitive to price, also started to buy cheaper tickets because the difference was large. This suggest that the airline has been losing its most profitable customers. A better approach might be to use dynamic pricing, which adjust fares according to demand and time before departure. Such systems are widely used in the industry and can increase yield without making the basic fare too low.

We recommend that the airline introduce three fare classes with clear benefits, such as baggage and seat selection, and monitor booking patterns for six months. It should also negotiate with the unions to create a more flexible cost structure for off peak routes. In our view, the company cannot win a pure price war against low cost carriers, so it must focus on the segments where service quality and schedule reliability create real value for customers.

prompt: Write a case analysis on supply chain disruption for a home improvement retailer.
text:
Harcourt Home, a national chain of home improvement stores with 140 outlets, experienced a significant disruption to its supply chain in the second half of 2024 when a key port terminal closed for an extended period. This case analysis evaluates the company's response to the disruption, the trade-offs embedded in its sourcing strategy, and the implications for its medium term operational resilience. The firm had historically relied on a lean inventory model, supported by a small number of primary suppliers located in a single region, which had delivered considerable cost efficiencies. The closure exposed the vulnerability of this configuration, as stock levels in several product categories fell below safety thresholds within three weeks.

The management team responded by activating emergency air freight for high margin items, renegotiating allocations with alternative suppliers, and temporarily reducing the range of products offered online. These measures stabilised availability for core categories but increased logistics costs by approximately 9 percent in the quarter. The response was broadly effective, although the analysis suggests that decisions were taken largely reactively and that the company lacked a formal contingency framework. The disruption also revealed weaknesses in the company's visibility of tier two suppliers, which limited its ability to anticipate shortages in raw materials.

Recommendations focus on diversifying the supplier base, establishing regional buffer inventories for critical lines, and investing in supply chain data systems that provide earlier warning of disruption. While these measures would increase working capital requirements and modestly reduce unit margins, they are likely to yield net benefits given the frequency of similar events in recent years. Management should present these options to the board with a clear cost benefit analysis and a timetable for implementation.

prompt: Business case analysis of a coffee subscription startup.
text:
Okay so this case is about a small startup called Beanwise that sells coffee subscriptions. The founders started it in a spare room with about 2,000 dollars, and within two years they had around 3,500 subscribers. That sounds great, but the case is really about whether the business can actually make money. Their monthly churn rate is about 9 percent, which means they lose almost one in ten customers every month, and acquiring a new customer costs them roughly 65 dollars through ads. The average subscriber pays 22 dollars a month, so the maths is pretty tight once you take shipping and roasting costs into account.

The founders have three options on the table. They could keep spending on paid ads and hope the customer lifetime value goes up. They could raise prices, which might help margins but could push people to cancel even faster. Or they could focus on retention, like offering flexible plans, better product variety and a referral program. Honestly, the retention option looks the most promising to me. The cost of keeping someone is way lower than finding a new person, and customers who stay for a year or more are much more profitable. The data also suggests that people who try three or more different roasts are the least likely to leave.

My take is that Beanwise should stop spending so much on ads for a few months and put that money into a better onboarding experience and a rotating menu. They should also track churn by cohort so they can see exactly when people drop off. If they can bring churn down to around 5 percent, the business starts to look a lot healthier. I'm not sure they will get there, but it's a much better bet than pouring more cash into ads that don't seem to pay off.

prompt: Write a history essay on the Marshall Plan.
text:
The Marshall Plan, formally the European Recovery Program, was an American initiative announced in June 1947 to provide economic assistance to Western Europe after the Second World War. Between 1948 and 1952 the United States transferred approximately 13 billion dollars in grants and loans to sixteen participating countries, a sum that amounted to a significant proportion of their combined national income. Historians have long debated the motives behind the programme. Traditional accounts emphasised humanitarian concern and the desire to prevent economic collapse, while revisionist scholars argued that the plan served American commercial interests and was designed to contain Soviet influence in Europe. Both interpretations contain elements of truth, and the most persuasive recent work treats the Marshall Plan as an instrument that combined generosity with strategic calculation.

The economic effects of the programme are difficult to isolate, since European recovery was already underway by the time aid arrived in significant quantities. Nevertheless, the aid helped to stabilise currencies, finance imports of raw materials and modernise industrial equipment. Equally important was the requirement that recipients cooperate with one another, which led to the creation of the Organisation for European Economic Co-operation, a precursor to later integration efforts. The plan thus contributed to a broader political shift in which European governments began to think in regional rather than purely national terms.

The Marshall Plan also had significant political consequences. Its conditions were used to pressure European governments to limit the role of communist parties in coalitions, and the Soviet Union responded by rejecting the aid and establishing the Molotov Plan for Eastern Europe. The division of the continent that followed was therefore shaped in part by the offer itself. Assessing the plan today requires holding these motives and outcomes together, recognising that it was simultaneously a humanitarian intervention, an economic stimulus and an early episode in the Cold War.

prompt: Write a history essay on the Chernobyl disaster.
text:
The Chernobyl disaster happened on 26 April 1986 at the nuclear power plant in Soviet Ukraine. During a safety test on reactor number four, the operators made a lot of mistakes and the reactor went out of control. There was a huge power surge and then two explosions, which blew the roof off the building and released radioactive material into the air. The explosion killed two workers immediately, and many more died in the following weeks from acute radiation sickness. The plant is near the city of Pripyat, which was evacuated a day and a half later, although the government did not announce anything to the public until days after the accident, when radiation was detected in Sweden.

The reason the disaster happened is important for understanding the history. The reactor design, called RBMK, had a flaw that made the power unstable at low levels, and the control rods had a graphite tip that made things worse at first. The test was poorly planned and the staff turned off several safety systems. But the essay I read argues that the blame should not just fall on the operators, because the Soviet system rewarded secrecy and punished people who reported problems. Engineers who raised concerns earlier were ignored, and the whole culture made it hard for anyone to say the reactor was unsafe.

The consequences were huge. Thirty one people died in the short term, and the long term health effects are still debated, with estimates ranging widely. A large area around the plant is still an exclusion zone. Many historians think Chernobyl helped push the Soviet Union towards glasnost, because the government had to admit what happened, and this openness contributed to the political changes that led to the collapse of the USSR a few years later. For me, the disaster shows how technical failure and political secrecy can combine to create a catastrophe.

prompt: Write a history essay on the Bandung Conference of 1955.
text:
The Bandung Conference, held in April 1955 in Indonesia, was one of the first major meetings of newly independent states from Asia and Africa. Twenty nine countries took part, many of which had only recently gained independence from European colonial rule. The conference was organised by five countries, including Indonesia, India and Burma, and it aimed to promote economic and cultural cooperation while opposing colonialism in all its forms. Its importance lies in the fact that it gave these countries a collective voice in international affairs at a time when the world was divided between the United States and the Soviet Union.

The conference produced the Final Communique, which contain ten principles, including respect for sovereignty, non interference in internal affairs and peaceful settlement of disputes. These principles became the basis for the later Non Aligned Movement, which was formally established in Belgrade in 1961. Some historians argue that Bandung was more symbolic than practical, because the participants had very different political systems and many disagreements were not resolved. For example, the relationship between China and India was tense, and the discussions about communism was difficult. Nevertheless, the meeting showed that the Global South could organise itself without depending on either superpower.

In my opinion, the Bandung Conference is an important event that is often neglected in Western history books. It challenged the idea that international politics was only about the Cold War blocs. It also gave new confidence to anti colonial movements in Africa, several of which were still fighting for independence in the late 1950s. Although its direct results were limited, the conference offered a vision of solidarity and sovereignty that influenced diplomacy for decades afterwards.

prompt: Write a history essay on the Great Depression and the New Deal.
text:
The economic collapse that began in 1929 produced the most severe downturn in the modern history of the United States, with unemployment reaching roughly a quarter of the labour force by 1933. The crisis exposed the inadequacy of existing governmental responses, which had been predicated on the assumption that markets would self-correct, and it prompted a fundamental reconsideration of the relationship between the federal government and the economy. Franklin D. Roosevelt's New Deal, introduced after his inauguration in 1933, represented an unprecedented expansion of federal authority, encompassing financial regulation, public employment, agricultural adjustment and the establishment of social insurance. Its significance lies less in any single programme than in the principle that the state bore responsibility for economic security.

Historians continue to debate the effectiveness of these measures. Some scholars emphasise the success of institutions such as the Securities and Exchange Commission and the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation in restoring confidence, arguing that they addressed structural weaknesses that had contributed to the crisis. Others contend that the recovery was incomplete until the mobilisation for the Second World War, and that certain policies, including the National Recovery Administration, may have impeded growth by restricting competition. The debate is complicated by the difficulty of separating the effects of deliberate policy from the broader trajectory of the economy.

What is less contested is the lasting political legacy of the period. The New Deal established a durable coalition and created programmes, notably Social Security, that became fixed features of American life. It also shifted expectations about what citizens could reasonably demand from their government. Although the scope of federal intervention has since been contested, the reforms of the 1930s remain a reference point in subsequent debates about the proper role of the state, and any assessment of the period must therefore account for both its immediate achievements and its enduring influence on political thought.

prompt: Write a history essay on the fall of the Berlin Wall.
text:
Okay so the fall of the Berlin Wall is one of those events everyone knows about, but I didn't really get why it mattered until I looked into the details. The wall went up in 1961 to stop East Germans from leaving for the West, and for almost three decades it was the most visible symbol of the Cold War. By 1989 though, things were changing fast. Hungary had already opened its border with Austria over the summer, and thousands of East Germans were escaping that way. The East German government was under pressure, and people were protesting in cities like Leipzig every Monday.

What happened on 9 November was kind of an accident. A spokesman named Günter Schabowski gave a press conference and said, pretty confusingly, that new travel rules would take effect immediately. He didn't actually know the details, and when journalists pushed him on when the rules started, he sort of waved his hands and said as far as he knew, right away. So that evening crowds showed up at the checkpoints, and the guards, who had no real orders, eventually just opened the gates. People started climbing on the wall and hammering pieces off it. It was chaotic and really emotional.

Looking back, I think the big lesson is that a lot of historic change comes from messy moments like this rather than clean plans. Nobody in the East German leadership had intended the wall to fall that night, but the situation had built up for months and one mistake tipped it over. It also led pretty fast to German reunification in 1990, and then the whole Soviet bloc started falling apart. I found it kind of wild that something so huge could come down to a press conference that went wrong. Definitely a good reminder that history isn't always as planned as the textbooks make it seem.

prompt: Write an argumentative essay on how autonomous vehicles should handle unavoidable crash decisions.
text:
The so-called trolley problem has become a popular reference point in discussions about autonomous vehicles, yet the comparison is often misleading. In the classic thought experiment, a bystander must decide whether to divert a runaway tram onto a track where it will kill one person instead of five. Engineers designing self-driving cars, however, do not face a single dramatic choice with a known outcome. Their systems operate under uncertainty, with imperfect sensors and probabilistic predictions about pedestrians and other drivers. This essay argues that autonomous vehicles should minimise overall risk through conservative, rule-consistent behaviour rather than explicit calculations about which individuals to sacrifice, and that the relevant moral reasoning concerns accountability and public trust more than philosophical dilemmas.

The strongest objection to this position holds that a system which avoids explicit harm calculations is still making value judgements, since decisions about braking distance and lane positioning inevitably affect who is hurt. This objection is correct as far as it goes. However, it does not follow that designers should attempt to encode a hierarchy of lives. Such hierarchies would be difficult to justify publicly, would invite legal challenges and would likely be exploited by manufacturers seeking to market their cars as safer for particular groups. A system that follows transparent rules, such as obeying speed limits and maintaining safe following distances, distributes risk in a way that can be audited and debated, which seems preferable to opaque optimisation.

The second part of the argument concerns responsibility. When a collision occurs, society needs to know who is accountable, whether the manufacturer, the software developer or the owner. Clear rules make this assessment possible, whereas an algorithm that chooses between victims would create serious difficulties for courts and insurers. For these reasons, I conclude that the most ethical approach is to design vehicles that prioritise predictable, law-abiding behaviour and to focus regulatory effort on testing, transparency and liability rather than on hypothetical dilemmas.

prompt: Argue whether scientists should be allowed to edit human embryos.
text:
Should scientists be allowed to edit the genes of human embryos? This question has become more urgent since the development of CRISPR, a tool that can change DNA sequences quickly and cheaply. In my opinion, embryo editing should be allowed only for serious inherited diseases, under strict regulation, and not for enhancing traits like intelligence or height. My main reason is that the risks to future people who cannot consent are very high, and we do not yet know enough about how edits might affect other genes over time.

The people who support wider use argue that it would be wrong to refuse a treatment that could prevent suffering. If a couple carries a gene for something like cystic fibrosis, editing the embryo could mean the child never has the disease. Some philosophers also say that parents have a right to make reproductive choices, and that banning a technology is a kind of paternalism. I think these arguments are strong, and I agree that there is a difference between preventing a disease and making a healthy child better. But the problem is that the line between treatment and enhancement is not always clear, and once the technology exists it could be hard to stop people from pushing it further.

There is also a fairness issue. If only rich families can afford editing, it might create a biological gap between social classes, which would make inequality worse. Because of this, I think governments should make a clear legal framework that allows research and limited clinical use for severe conditions, while banning enhancement. Scientists should also be open about their results, and there should be public debate before any major step is taken. Overall, I believe that editing embryos can be ethically acceptable, but only if we are careful about who it helps and what it is used for.

prompt: Write an argumentative essay on keeping animals in zoos.
text:
Keeping wild animals in zoos is one of the most debated ethical questions in modern society. Supporters argue that zoos protect endangered species, provide education for the public and fund conservation projects in the wild. These benefits are real, and many zoos have successful breeding programmes for species such as the California condor. However, the question is not only about what zoos can achieve, but also about whether it is right to keep animals in captivity for human entertainment. This essay will argue that zoos can only be justified when they meet strict standards of welfare and when they focus on conservation rather than display.

The main reason is that captivity restricts the natural behaviour of many animals. Large carnivores need to hunt and travel long distances, and elephants live in complex social groups that cannot be easily reproduced in a small enclosure. Studies have shown that animals in poor conditions can show stress behaviour, such as repetitive pacing or self-harm. Some critics say that even good zoos cannot prevent these problems completely, because the animal is always in an artificial environment. In my view, this objection is strong, and it suggests that large numbers of species should not be kept in zoos at all.

On the other hand, the defenders of zoos say that many animals would not survive in the wild anyway, because of habitat loss and poaching. Without zoos, some species might be extinct. I accept that this is a serious point. Yet this argument only works if zoos really do invest in conservation and release animals when possible. Therefore I believe the best position is to support zoos that are transparent about their welfare, that contribute to field research and that keep only species they can care for properly. Other zoos should be closed.

prompt: Write an argumentative essay on whether governments should tax accumulated wealth.
text:
The question of whether governments should impose annual taxes on accumulated wealth, rather than relying solely on taxes on income and transactions, has received renewed attention in recent years. This essay contends that a moderately progressive wealth tax is justified on grounds of distributive justice and democratic legitimacy, although its practical design must address legitimate concerns about valuation, capital flight and administrative cost. The argument proceeds in three stages: first, it considers the normative case that large concentrations of wealth can distort political equality; second, it evaluates the empirical objections raised by critics; and third, it outlines the conditions under which such a tax could be implemented effectively.

The normative case begins from the observation that wealth confers power that is not fully captured by income. Individuals with substantial capital holdings can influence public policy through lobbying, philanthropy and control of media, and their economic position may allow them to avoid taxes that fall on earned income. Taxing accumulated wealth therefore serves not merely to raise revenue but to limit the translation of economic advantage into political influence. Critics respond that such a tax penalises saving and entrepreneurship, yet this objection assumes that the marginal rate applied to the very largest fortunes would meaningfully reduce investment, a claim that the evidence does not clearly support.

The practical objections deserve serious attention. Valuing illiquid assets such as private businesses and art is notoriously difficult, and wealthy individuals may relocate to avoid liability. These problems are real, but they are not insurmountable. Comprehensive reporting requirements, international information exchange and a generous threshold that excludes ordinary households can mitigate both administrative burden and avoidance. Accordingly, I conclude that a wealth tax, if carefully designed and internationally coordinated, represents a legitimate instrument for promoting a fairer and more democratic distribution of resources.

prompt: Argumentative essay: should anonymous accounts be banned on social media?
text:
Should people be allowed to post online under fake names? I used to say no without thinking much about it, but after reading a bit more I'm not so sure anymore. Some people argue that anonymity makes everyone worse, because nobody has to own what they say, and that's where trolling and harassment come from. There's definitely something to that. But I think banning anonymity would cause more problems than it solves, so my view is that anonymous accounts should stay legal, while platforms get better at punishing abuse no matter whether the account has a real name or not.

The strongest reason for anonymity is that it protects people who are vulnerable. Think about someone who is LGBTQ and not out to their family, or a whistleblower exposing a company, or a survivor of abuse who wants to talk about it without everyone in their town finding out. For these people, a real name can be dangerous. If governments or platforms required real IDs, those people would be the first to get hurt, especially in countries where speaking up can get you arrested. Honestly, I think that's a pretty big deal, and it's the thing that changed my mind.

Of course the counterargument is that anonymous accounts are used for the worst stuff, like coordinated harassment campaigns. That's true, but the answer isn't really to take away the anonymity. Platforms can limit how quickly new accounts post, detect bot networks, and make it easier to report abuse and get action. They can also be held responsible for not acting. So to me the question isn't real name versus fake name, it's whether the platform takes responsibility for what happens on it. I think that's the more honest way to deal with the problem.

prompt: Write a summary of a research proposal on federated learning for hospital readmission prediction.
text:
This proposal investigates the use of federated learning to develop predictive models for hospital readmission risk without requiring the centralisation of patient records. Hospitals hold detailed clinical data that could improve care if combined, yet privacy regulation and institutional policy make pooling datasets difficult. Federated learning offers an alternative in which local models are trained on each institution's data and only parameter updates are shared with a central aggregator. The project will assess whether such an approach can achieve predictive performance comparable to a centralised model while providing stronger guarantees about data locality. Its primary contribution will be a systematic evaluation of the trade-offs between accuracy, communication cost and robustness to heterogeneous patient populations across participating sites.

The methodology combines three components. First, a standardised feature set will be derived from electronic health records across five partner hospitals, using a common data model to address differences in coding practices. Second, the study will compare federated averaging with a secure aggregation protocol and a differentially private variant, measuring how each affects model performance and privacy leakage. Third, the evaluation will test whether models trained on data from larger hospitals generalise to smaller sites with different case mixes. Performance will be measured using area under the curve, calibration error and fairness metrics across demographic subgroups. Experiments will be run on a simulated federation before deployment in a live environment, which reduces the risk of exposing real patient information during development.

The expected outcomes include a reproducible open source framework, a set of empirical benchmarks and guidance for hospitals considering similar collaborations. The project is limited by the availability of data partners and by the computational cost of secure aggregation at scale, both of which are addressed in the risk section. If successful, the work will help establish federated learning as a practical option for clinical prediction in environments where data sharing is constrained by law or institutional trust.

prompt: Summarise your proposal for a code review bot for first year programming assignments.
text:
My project is about building a code review bot that gives feedback to first year students on their programming assignments. Right now students get their marks back weeks after submitting, and by then they have forgotten what they wrote. The idea is that the bot runs automatically when a student pushes code to the course repository, and it checks for common problems like unused variables, poor naming, missing comments and simple logic errors. It will not give the answer, but it will point out where to look and explain why something might be wrong. I want to see whether fast feedback helps students improve their code before the final submission.

To build it I plan to use a combination of existing linting tools and a language model that has been fine tuned on past student submissions. The linting tools are good at catching style issues but they cannot explain things in plain language, so the model would translate the warnings into more helpful comments. I will collect around 300 anonymised submissions from last years course and label common mistakes by hand. The bot will be tested on a separate set of code so I can measure how often its comments are correct and useful. I also need to think about how to keep the feedback from being too harsh, since first years can get discouraged easily.

The evaluation will have two parts. Technically I will measure precision, meaning how many of the comments are actually correct, and recall, meaning how many real problems it finds. For the user side, I want to run a small study with volunteers from the next cohort and ask them whether the feedback was helpful. I expect some limits, for example the bot might be wrong sometimes or students might just copy its suggestions without understanding them. If the project works, the department could use it as a free teaching assistant that is available at any time of the day.

prompt: Write a research proposal summary on speech recognition for low-resource languages.
text:
This research proposal present a study on automatic speech recognition for low resource languages, with a particular focus on Kyrgyz. Most speech recognition systems are trained on large datasets of English, Mandarin and a few other languages, which means that speakers of smaller languages often receive poor service. The goal of this project is to develop a system that can achieve useful accuracy with only a few hours of transcribed audio. We will use self supervised pre training on unlabelled recordings collected from radio archives, and then fine tune the model on a smaller set of carefully annotated speech. The aim is to show that the gap between high resource and low resource languages can be reduced with more efficient methods.

The research will be divided into three phases. In the first phase, we will collect and clean audio data, and we will also work with native speakers to check transcription guidelines. Dialect variation is a big challenge, because Kyrgyz has several regional accents that can change pronunciation a lot. In the second phase, we will compare different pre training approaches and measure how the word error rate changes when the amount of labelled data is reduced. In the third phase, we will test the system with real users, such as journalists and teachers, who can give feedback on usability. We think this user involvement is important, because a model that works well on benchmarks may still be unhelpful in practice.

We expect the project to produce an open dataset, a trained model and a set of recommendations for other researchers working with small languages. There are also ethical considerations, especially about the ownership of the recordings and the consent of speakers whose voices appear in the archives. We will address these by consulting community representatives and by following data governance principles. We believe the study will contribute to making language technology more inclusive, and that it can serve as a template for other communities facing similar problems.

prompt: Write a research proposal summary on consistency in geo-replicated distributed databases.
text:
This proposal sets out a programme of research into the consistency guarantees offered by geo-replicated distributed databases under conditions of partial network failure. Contemporary systems frequently offer a choice between strong consistency and low latency, yet the practical implications of this trade-off remain poorly characterised for many workloads. The research will develop a formal model of consistency anomalies that arise under asynchronous replication and will evaluate their frequency in production-like environments. The principal objective is to produce a methodology that allows system designers to determine, with greater precision, which anomalies are tolerable for a given application and which require coordination at the cost of availability.

The methodology comprises three stages. The first stage involves the specification of a labelled transition system describing replica behaviour, from which safety properties relevant to common application patterns will be derived. The second stage employs fault injection within a controlled testbed to observe the occurrence of violations under varying partition durations and replication topologies. The third stage applies model checking to verify that the proposed coordination strategies satisfy the derived properties. The use of both empirical and formal techniques is intended to ensure that conclusions are grounded in observed behaviour and are not merely theoretical.

The anticipated contributions include a taxonomy of anomalies with associated detection procedures, an open source testing harness and a set of design guidelines for practitioners. The principal risk concerns the state space explosion inherent in model checking large systems, which will be mitigated through abstraction and compositional reasoning. The findings are expected to inform both the academic study of distributed systems and the engineering decisions made by organisations that depend upon replicated data stores for mission critical operations.

prompt: Write a proposal summary for a browser extension that detects phishing.
text:
So my proposal is basically a browser extension that tries to spot phishing sites before you type in your password. Phishing is still one of the most common ways people get hacked, and the fake login pages look more and more real every year. The extension would check the URL, look at things like weird domain names and recently registered sites, and compare the page layout to the real brand's login page. If something looks off, it shows a warning. Nothing too crazy, but I think the interesting part is the layout comparison, because most existing tools only look at blacklists, which are always a bit behind.

For the technical side I'm planning to use a lightweight model that runs locally in the browser, so that users' browsing history doesn't get sent to a server. That's a big deal for privacy. I'll use Manifest V3 since Chrome requires it now, and I'll test on a dataset of known phishing pages that a security group already collected. I also want to measure how often the extension gives false alarms, because if it warns people too much, they'll just click through without reading. Honestly, that false alarm problem is probably the hardest part of the whole project.

If it works, I'd like to release it as open source so other people can check the code. The main risks are that attackers adapt quickly and that the model might be slow on older laptops. I'm hoping to keep the extension small and fast, and to write a clear explanation of what it does and doesn't check. Overall I think it's a practical project that could actually help people who aren't security experts, which is the main reason I wanted to do it.

prompt: Write speaker notes for a marketing presentation launching a reusable insulated water bottle.
text:
Good morning everyone, and thank you for joining us. Today I want to walk you through the launch plan for our new insulated water bottle, the Summit 750. Before we look at the product itself, it is worth noting the context. Single-use plastic bottles remain one of the most visible sources of household waste, and a growing number of consumers now say they want reusable alternatives. However, many reusable bottles on the market are either expensive or poorly designed, so our challenge is to deliver something that performs well and still feels good value.

Moving to the product, the Summit 750 keeps drinks cold for up to 24 hours and uses a leak-proof lid that has passed independent testing. Please note that the 24-hour claim is based on ice water tested at room temperature, and I would advise us to present it as up to 24 hours in all external materials. The bottle is made from recycled stainless steel and is designed to fit standard car cup holders, which our research identified as a key purchase factor for commuters. On this slide, the price point of 32 dollars places it in the mid-range, and our competitive analysis shows it undercuts the leading premium brand by roughly 20 percent.

For the launch itself, our plan focuses on three channels. We will begin with a targeted social media campaign aimed at adults aged 25 to 40 who already buy reusable products, followed by partnerships with outdoor retailers and gyms. Our final phase is a referral programme that rewards customers for recommending the bottle to friends. We will measure success through sell-through rate, repeat purchase intent and social engagement. prompt: Write speaker notes for a strategic review of a luxury skincare brand repositioning.
text:
Good morning, and thank you for attending this strategic review of the Aurelia skincare range. My objective today is to present the rationale for repositioning the brand within the prestige segment, together with the associated communication plan for the coming financial year. The current positioning emphasises clinical efficacy, a message that has served the brand well with dermatology-referred consumers but has limited its appeal among younger affluent customers, who increasingly seek sensory experience alongside demonstrable results. The proposed repositioning therefore seeks to integrate scientific credibility with a more immersive brand narrative, without diluting the evidence that underpins our claims.

Turning to the market evidence, our analysis indicates that growth in the prestige skincare category has been concentrated in products that combine ingredient transparency with ritual, rather than in those that rely solely on technical claims. Consumer panels reveal that purchasers in the 28 to 38 age bracket place considerable value on packaging, tactile experience and the perceived integrity of the company. Accordingly, we propose a three-part strategy: refining the visual identity to communicate restraint and craftsmanship, introducing a limited series of ritual-based treatments, and expanding our educational content on ingredient sourcing. Each element is designed to strengthen the link between scientific rigour and aesthetic appeal.

Financially, the repositioning requires an incremental investment of approximately 4.2 million in product development, creative production and launch activity over eighteen months. The projected return rests on a modest increase in average selling price and a measurable improvement in customer retention within the target cohort. I recommend that the committee approve phase one of the programme, subject to a review of early performance indicators at the six-month point. I would welcome your questions on any aspect of the proposal.
